Title: Watford tourney/Temptation of Greater Sleaze/Ultimate refutation of CL

Messages.Author: legbiter
Messages.Body:
It was great to finally meet Sorrow this weekend. He arrived early
Saturday afternoon and after a quick pizza he, Michael and i beetled
off to Southampton to play in the Final Nights sealed-deck tourney. We
were a bit late but 6 of us played 2 3-player tables. i had the
Giovanni at our table, preying on Chris's Setites and being preyed
upon by an Assamite deck whose owner's name i didn't catch. No
drafting was allowed but nobody said you couldn't take cards out, so i
trimmed the Spaghetti-sucking Corpse-fucking crimbos of all their crap
cards and swept our table quite comfortably. Sorrow reckons i cheated
by taking cards out, which is true but i cheated legally in being
quicker on abusing the literal text of the rules than anybody else. So
there. Michael had a slightly harder time at his table cos he had the
Ravnos, but eventually he swept, too. So we rolled a dice to see who
won, and it was Michael [aka Anklebiter aged 12]. This cheered him up
quite a bit after his recent poor run of form and not being able to go
to the Watford tourneys because they are in a pub. It also makes him
the youngest AND the second-youngest person ever to have won a
competitive VTES event.

Then we had a barbie [mmmm .... dioxins ....] and afterwards i taught
Sorrow how to play New Rage. It was a terrific game, and when the fur
and squidgy bits had ceased to fly Sorrow's Get of Fenris were the
victors over Michael's Bone Gnawers and my Silent Striders. Good fun!

Next day Sorrow, John Eagles and i made the trek up to Watford for a
nice big tourney, 22 or so people IIRC. Rob was there briefly but did
not play, Barney and Will being other notable absentees. It was good
to see james Coupe back in the competitive frame and playing what Matt
and i think is his best deck ever. Sorrow played a storming weenie
obfuscate-embrace deck for 9 VPs and i played a totally new deck which
i threw together that morning, for 10VPs in the heats and 1 in the
final. i call this deck Temptation of Greater Sleaze; the design
principle being quite simply to include as many as possible of the
cards that make your heart sink when they hit the table. Here's the
deck, with notes to indicate where i think it could be modified for
the better:

DECK NAME: TEMPTATION OF GREATER SLEAZE

CRYPT [12 vampires]
Zebulon [replace with Mariel]
Leandro x 2
Lucian x 4
Greger Anderssen x 2
Gilbert Duane x 2

LIBRARY
MASTERS [21]
Direct Intervention
Dreams of the Sphinx
Giant's blood
Golconda - Inner Peace
Information Highway
Legendary Vampire
Minion Tap x 4
The Parthenon
Pentex Subversion
Temptation of Greater Power x 4
Tomb of Rameses III x 3
Secure Haven
Sudden Reversal
ACTIONS [9]
The Fifth Tradition: Hospitality x 3
Govern the Unaligned x 2
Kine Dominance x 2
Pulse of the Canaille
Revelations [remove]
VOTES [18]
Anarchist Uprising x 2
Ancient Influence
Banishment x 2
Dramatic Upheaval
KRC x 5
Parity Shift x 4
Political flux [maybe remove]
Political Stranglehold
Rabble Razing [remove]
REACTIONS [20]
Deflection x 4
Forced Awakening
Obedience x 4
The Second Tradition: Domain x 2
Telepathic Counter x 3 [not sure. Maybe remove].
WWEF x 6
ACTION MODIFIERS [22]
Cloak the Gathering x 4
Conditioning x 3
Elder impersonation
Faceless Night x 4
Forgotten Labyrinth
Lost in Crowds x 4
Spying Mission
Swallowed by the Night x 4

[Yep, not a Happy Families deck and NO combat cards. What, i can't
break my own rules from time to time? You wait till you see the NEXT
emanation of the Legbitery grey matter!!!!]

Odd tournament this one. i got 4VP in the first 5-player game, getting
early vote-lock and pulling off Parity Shift, Deflection and Anarchist
Uprising plus some biggish bleeds. LOTS of weenies on the table.
Second game [4-player] i swept thanks to Dramatic Upheaval, KRC,
Banishment, big bleeds, wake/Obedience, ToGP [14-point master-phase
bleed], and mariel's special. Third game [4-player] i tied, despite
having TWO fears of Mekhet played on me by my second prey [i suddened
one of them]; i did another 14-point master-phase bleed with ToGP on
Daniel Vandenberg in this one. In the final i chose to bleed Sorrow
and to be bled by Matt. i was doing OK until martin Cubberley did a
totally-ridiculous cross-table rush against Mariel. Yes, yes, i KNOW i
said that combat decks should do cross-table rushes against their
grand-prey in order to bring the table down to three and try to win
from there. Own, petard, hoist sorta thing. i still got Sorrow's scalp
but that was a self-oust; he was in a losing position and chose the
manner of his going [if not self-ousted he was going to die to Matthew
who had a Dramatic Upheaval in his hand which had been Delaying
Tactic'd the previous round]. i had Niki Sehmi down to 5 pool with a
Kine Dominance, Conditioning and LOADS of stealth in hand, but i tried
to be too clever and called a Parity Shift against my grand-prey
first. To my astonishment Matthew did me in with an Elder Kindred
Network! FANTASTIC tactical play. i hope it worked out for him
strategically, too, but i have my doubts - when i left he was alone on
the table with two combat decks. i was doing OK against the combat
decks even with Mariel in the bin - cos nothing about her card-text
says you can't use her special while she's in torpor, so i did. So,
once again i score top VPs for a tourney but don't win. Bah. John
reckons it is because the UK players are all scared of me that they do
all this ridiculous cross-table shit. Scaredy, scaredy, scaredy cats
and ya-boo stinky-poohs to those of you upon whom this cap fits.

In between the first and second heats Daniel Vandenberg and i played a
FN duel, his tweaked Giovanni vs my tweaked Assamites. Assamites won,
but it was tight - i was down to 1 pool. In between the third heat and
the final we played Fluxx and i won, apparently. And i traded for TWO
Your Sugarys, an Ex Nihilo and something else juicy, possibly a Sargon
fragment. So i had a good time overall and thanks, Dave, for another
dam' fine event. Sorrow didn't come back with us because his work was
taking him to Derby next day, but we look forward to entertaining him
again real soon!

Finally i note with some surprise that the deck i built is legal under
6-cl, and could easily be made so for 4CL [replace a KRC with
conservative agitation, and 2 wakes with Forced Awakening]. i repeat
that it won the most VPs in this tourney, and my experience of playing
it convinces me that in addition to being deadly it is flexible, fun
to play, tactically and strategically-challenging, and robust. i
emphasise that this was an official NCL tourney, sporting some
absolutely classical focussed-degenerate decks [including the
rush-deck type that rattles Andrew's cage so much - no problem with
that one thanks to Mariel and wake/obedience. It might be nice if
Sorrow could post his deck which most likely got the second-higgest
VPs so that people can see what i'm talking about when i mention
degeneracy. Chris, you up for that?]. Is it, i wonder, too much to
hope that the CL people will shut their traps now? If not, might they
at least have the humility to consider the possibility that their
deck-constructing and playing skills, rather than the game itself,
leave something to be desired?

Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson
Messages.Body:
On 26 Jun 2001 01:49:12 -0700, legbiter wrote:

>In handing his prey TWO VPs? i don't see how that qualifies as smart.

It depends what would have happened otherwise. He clearly took the
view that you were a menace and had to be taken down. The bottom line
is that he won and you lost. You are therefore not in a strong
position to make exaggerated claims for your deck, good as it may be.

>i don't see how on Caine's earth you come to this conclusion. i was
>playing a deck which was legal under CL. i got the most VPs in the
>tourney with 11.

This goes back to the issue of whether the object of the game is to
win or to maximise your VPs. Tom has seemed to go into these things
with a general plan of being the last man standing and scoring 2 VPs
to win the game.

>This means that the central argument of the CL
>people, that NCL makes it impossible for people with few copies of
>cards to compete, isn't true. i repeat. It ISN'T TRUE.

A straw man. I think the general complaint of the CL folk is that the
NCL metagame is dominated by boring, degenerate decks. If some decks
which don't fit that description are viable, this doesn't really solve
the problem. It's not that it's "impossible" to play a more moderate
deck, it's that it's difficult and hence most players don't do it.

I note btw that I couldn't build your deck as I don't have 4 copies of
ToGP. That makes it a power deck in my book - comparable with strong
decks in other CCG which use 4 copies of a power rare. Folk on the
shadowfist list are currently arguing about whether having 5 copies of
certain cards in a deck makes it cheesy and a bad thing. VTES is off
the scale from this point of view. I'm fairly agnostic about this
issue but am suspicious of the aggressive arguments coming from folk
who are so clearly "haves" rather than "have-nots". I've decided not
to be a "have" as it would soon get out of hand. I'm really not
interested in buying a case of Final Nights as it would be a major
PITA opening, sorting and organising that many cards. I've bought one
starter, a few boosters and will probably stop there. If I thought
that buying a box of boosters would give me enough cards then I might
go further but it wouldn't be anything like enough, would it?

>It did get quite busy, which isn't a completely bad thing. i
>accidentally scored with an agreeable person of the opposite gender
>just before the final, but obviously was quite unable to DO anything
>about it.

What, you mean she didn't want to play VTES <grin>?

Andrew

My take on FN is that I'm not very interested in the Independent clans
- they just lack sex appeal or something. There are a few cards that
I am interested in though - Jake Washington, for example. He's a card
that you can use several copies of but he's a rare. In other CCG,
you'd have some number of copies to shoot for. In Doomtown, I'm not
bothered if I only have one of a card - the decks are so tight and the
uniqueness rules are so tough. In Shadowfist, I like to have 5 of a
card - more can be nice to have but you know that you won't be using
them all in one deck. In VTES there is no such comfort factor. There
are several cards that I've come across that I know I'd want lots of
copies of if I played the game seriously (where lots means
double-figures). Some of these cards are rare or uncommon and that's
when I get cold feet.

If the game had been done differently, e.g. CL 6, no deck limit, and
special cards like Contract unlimited, then I'd be a lot more ready to
embrace it. I'm not convinced that the game would be all that
different in practise, much as you're saying about your deck. This
holy-war, don't-give-an-inch stuff does nothing to persuade me - the
arguments aren't as cut and dried as the NCL advocates make out.

Andrew

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <9ha1sm$ved$1...@nntp2-cm.news.eni.net>, Matt Latham
<mla...@diamondtoolmfg.com> writes

>Now come on... CL people aren't idiots. NCL people aren't idiots. Just
>different styles of play.

It's just one of the standard arguments:

"Look at this NCL deck I've just built. It's so whack. If we were
playing CL it'd be so much better....."

That's half the point. Just because you *can* do something under NCL
doesn't mean that you should, or that it will benefit you. There are
lots and lots and lots of potential decks you can build under NL, all of
which are utterly rubbish and which a sensible deck builder can cope
with with ease, no matter how many copies of a given card there are in a
deck.

The game is inherently self-limiting in many arenas - restrictions on
action modifiers, master cards, reactions, strikes, additional strikes,
maneuvers, presses, restrictions on playing stealth and intercept,
limitations on actions via NRA (part of the de facto rules set in most
environments) and such like.

Dealing with that requires a hugely intelligent and delicate
understanding of the state of play. The standard reactions of players
who have played CL and then get told that NL is the way to play doesn't
take into account all of this - precisely because playing CL doesn't
have all of these issues, due to the fact that these issues are an
inherent design decision (with the exception of NRA, which has been
intelligently, sensitively and carefully balanced over time) in the
construction of the game.

It's exactly what Richard Garfield intended, having seen what happened
with Magic. He assumed that most people would never have a full set,
and that 400 cards would be a *lot*. So V:TES works exactly the other
way. You can have *huge* numbers of cards, but it's in your interests
to balance it yourself. Too few, you can't do anything. Too many, you
hang yourself.

And the little bear said, "This deck is just right....."

takes just one win in a tournament rounds to annulate them.

Do you want to be BEST player in the world according to ratings ?

My method doesn´t require to win tournaments.
It even doesn´t require to go to the final.

All you need is to take a deck capable of doing 2/1/1/1 victory points
splits consistently. After three rounds you will have 6 VP which in
most tournaments I played recently 6 points was NOT sufficient to
guarantee you a place in the final. Yet you will gain around 180
points each tournaments. Repeat it in three tournaments and you will
have around 540 points gain. Assuming you started at 3000 you will end
with 3540 points which is about 200 points more than current top
player have. And you didn´t even went into the final in any single
tournament !

little bit different - your approach is to sweep two games out of
three in the preliminary rounds and then since you will probably have
most vp you will chose best position in the finals thus you will
probably win finals too. Sounds like a good plan , no ? You think that
you will have better ranking at the end than an 2/1/1/1 deck ? No !
You will only have gain of something like 120 points after each
tournament and around 360 after three tournament and this approach
require you to win three tournaments in the row which is way more
difficult than 2 vp per a game approach.

better than a player who has lower rating. Heck the one with lower
rating could be making finals regurarly and the one with bigger not.I

reward consistency - you can win three games and yet never go into the
finals but you will rightly be best player in the world after three
tournaments.

Conclusion : If we want to keep current tournament system we need to
change ratings.

If we want to keep ratings system we need to change tournament system.

This looks like a fine deck, though, FWIW, I can't make this one
either as I don't think I have any Miller/Art of Pain. Anyway, that's
another tick for the Toreadors which should keep them near the top of
the table.

>i note that this deck is also legal for 6CL. That's game, set and
>match as far as refuting Cl is concerned, i'd have thought.

Quite the reverse IMO. Both you and Martin can function quite well
within a 6CL. And I've seen many other decks which fit within this
constraint too. Some players even use this as a conscious parameter
when designing decks - stops them being too vulnerable to a nemesis.
So what's the big deal about having a 6CL?

This looks increasingly to me like an accident of history. Magic went
first with an arbitrary CL of 4 which worked out ok with the equally
arbitrary deck size of 60. VTES inherited the same CL in many groups
but this wasn't suitable for its larger decks. If a 6CL had been the
first choice for VTES, maybe that's what everyone would be playing
now, just as everyone now takes the 4CL limit for granted in Magic
even though it was grafted on to the original design too. Of course
you'd lose the amusing/degenerate decks which have 10+ copies of the
same card but all other CCG suffer this lack and seem to manage.

Andrew

Since 6CL decks are capable of beating an entire tourney-ful of NCL
decks, why limit the variety in the game by having an un-necessary
card limit? Many, many decks are simply not viable under 6CL and
never will be -- Corruption decks, Cryptic Mission decks, the list has
been restated endlessly.

Imposing an arbitrary card limit on the game for some nebulous concept
of "balance", especially when the game wasn't designed to be played
with a CL, is simply foolish on the face of it. Even more so when it
turns out that the "balance" isn't necessary - decks with 10+ of the
same card in them lose valuable flexibility that, at the highest
levels, is turning out to be necessary.

>This looks increasingly to me like an accident of history. Magic went
>first with an arbitrary CL of 4 which worked out ok with the equally
>arbitrary deck size of 60. VTES inherited the same CL in many groups
>but this wasn't suitable for its larger decks. If a 6CL had been the

V:TES inherited the same CL because it was another Garfield game, and
everyone just assumed that any Garfield game would have a CL. It is
interesting to note that 4CL in a 90-card deck does fall into that
particular trap as well.

Unless I'm mistaken, Magic didn't ORIGINALLY have a card limit - WotC
simply assumed that nobody would ever have that many of any given
card. Oops on their part, but it was a totally new field they were
entering, too. They had to bolt on patch after patch to the rules and
design afterwards to try to fix the problem.

>first choice for VTES, maybe that's what everyone would be playing
>now, just as everyone now takes the 4CL limit for granted in Magic
>even though it was grafted on to the original design too. Of course
>you'd lose the amusing/degenerate decks which have 10+ copies of the
>same card but all other CCG suffer this lack and seem to manage.

But the other CCGs were designed to have the card limits from the
ground up, which this wasn't. Magic's design has largely imploded on
itself over the years, and the 4CL has been a feature for so long that
it now truly IS being designed for 4CL.

-- Derek

Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson
Messages.Body:
On Wed, 27 Jun 2001 11:06:52 -0400, Derek Ray wrote:

>Unless I'm mistaken, Magic didn't ORIGINALLY have a card limit - WotC
>simply assumed that nobody would ever have that many of any given
>card. Oops on their part, but it was a totally new field they were
>entering, too. They had to bolt on patch after patch to the rules and
>design afterwards to try to fix the problem.

What gets forgotten in this debate is that VTES went through a similar
patching process. The game, as designed, could be broken and so
different groups adopted different house rules to fix it. Some went
with a CL like Magic while others went with Adrian Sullivan's Golden
Tenets - no repeat actions (NRA) and no vote pushing. The latter is
now regarded as orthodoxy but note that NRA still isn't in the
rulebook. I regard it with the same suspicion and distaste as you
regard a CL and for the same reason - that it wasn't in the original
design and isn't even a proper rule.

The Golden Tenet camp, personified by LSJ, have seized the levers of
power but it might not have gone that way. One year the big annual
tournament at Gencon was run by WotC with a 4CL, right? Supposing
that faction had taken the game forward. They might have fixed the
game to work well with a CL and folk who wanted to play without one
would now be the mavericks, raging against the system. What might
have been ...

Andrew

It puzzles me that NRA has not made it to the rulebook yet. With the
current design of the game and the way it's going, it seems a much
simpler course of action. Although I could suppose that things are
being left that way so as to not legislate older playgroups out of
existence.

>would now be the mavericks, raging against the system. What might

... is merely idle speculation. =)

I will note that the CL house rules adopted by many groups were
"glued-on" without thinking, in some cases without even realizing that
the game was NCL by design. OTOH, The Golden Tenets were crafted with
a significant amount of thought and time spent. In general, I'm going
to learn towards something that's had EFFORT put into it as more
likely to be "right" as opposed to a snap judgement.

-- Derek

I don't think NCL is bad for the play of the game as the game has been designed
to have no limits.

However, this (separate) point about owning cards being less desirable because
of NCL, IMO, has some validity. Some CCGers, such as myself, have the
mentality of having enough cards to build any deck that they might want to
build. That's not possible with NCL. (I find that I have a very hard time
trading because there's really almost nothing I'd want to give up as I might
find a use for it some day.)

While the game had done a good job of making commons among the best cards, I
believe that potential players are often daunted by how many cards they
wouldn't have that they could use (if only for greater variety).

If I were to put a new CCG on the market, I'd definitely feature CL. I bring
this up because what I don't like hearing is how a CCG is inherently inferior
because it has CL, which I hear occasionally from some of the locals. Still,
I'm not seeing the point in arguing CL for V:TES. It should have already
settled into "we agree to disagree, let's move on" years ago.

Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson

On 27 Jun 2001 13:23:58 -0700, Joshua Duffin wrote:

>In general, card limits in CCGs are an attempt to limit the effect of
>broken cards. Games that don't have broken cards don't need a CL.
>Shadowfist has been played - in fact I think you've even done it, if
>I remember right - without using its official 5CL and found to be
>fairly balanced even without limits. Likewise, VTES doesn't need a
>limit to be balanced. So why impose one on it?

Apart from setting a ceiling for a play set and eliminating monotonous
decks, I'd say because the lack of a CL forces you to errata cards
more frequently. A good example is Wake with Evening's Freshness
which got an ugly errata. The reason for this was some concern about
being able to pack large numbers of them which you could freely cycle
out of your hand. If the game had had a CL then this wouldn't have
been necessary.

The thing about CCGs is that tournament players are often totally
ruthless about breaking the game. If there's even the slightest
weakness in the game system they will push on it until it breaks. I
know this because I do it myself. A CL provides a safety net for
stuff that isn't caught in playtest and that's why every single CCG
apart from VTES has one. That's certainly why Shadowfist has one -
the designer said so himself. He thought that the game might work
without one but played it safe. Having thought about it, I'm fairly
sure that he's wrong and I backed away from running a NCL event. The
game would work fine for the most part with NCL but that's not good
enough - players would instantly seize on the parts that weren't fine
and destroy the game with them.

Oh, and another thing. If there were a CL then you'd be able to ditch
the other CL which VTES does have - the limit on deck size. It really
is a joke this, you know. You guys bang on and on about not having a
CL when there is, in fact, a very rigid limit on the number of cards
that you may put in your deck, i.e. 90 in tournament play. That's a
CL that Shadowfist doesn't have and it's great. My last
tournament-winning deck had 196 cards in it and is lots of fun to play
in consequence. This lack of a deck limit means that, unlike VTES,
there is a genuinely infinite number of decks that you can construct.
VTES supposed variety seems like a straight-jacket by comparison.

Doomtown takes yet another approach. There is a tight CL of 4 and a
fixed deck size of 52. But you can recycle your discards and so you
may draw and play a given card a potentially infinite number of times.
This is a whole new ball game and has the great merit that you are
mostly unlikely to run dry as can happen in the other two games.

Still, there's a lot to be said for VTES taking a different approach
too - it'd be dull if these CCG had identical mechanics. Just be
aware that there is a rich universe of possibilities out there and
there's something to be said for them all.

Andrew

prevents errata is by making sure that cards that need a fixing don't come up
as often.

>>A good example is Wake with Evening's Freshness which got an ugly errata.
The reason for this was some concern about being able to pack large numbers of
them which you could freely cycle out of your hand.>>

Wake was fixed because it had an effect that far outweighed its cost. VTES is a
game that is all about cost and effect. If you have a card that does has no
cost for its effect, it needs a fixing.

>>If the game had had a CL then this wouldn't have been necessary.>>

I fail to see how you come to this conclusion. Even if you have only 4 of them,
they still have an effect that vastly outweighs its cost. Thus they need
fixing. Just like when it was determined that Lightning Bolt had an effect that
vastly outweighed its cost in Magic. They had a 4CL, and *still* had to turn
Lightning Bolt into Incinerate.

>>A CL provides a safety net for stuff that isn't caught in playtest and that's
why every single CCG apart from VTES has one.>>

No, it is 'cause they are designed to have a CL. VTES was specifically designed
to not have a CL.

>>That's certainly why Shadowfist has one -the designer said so himself.>>

Yup, and as a result, the cards are made assuming a card limit. In VTES, the
cards are designed assuming no card limit. If you suddenly impose one, you are
forcing cards that are designed to work without a CL into a CL framework. If
they were designed to work under a CL from day one, that would be fine. As it
is, however, the very basis of the game is that it is designed for no card
limit.

>>Oh, and another thing. If there were a CL then you'd be able to ditch
the other CL which VTES does have - the limit on deck size.>>

This strikes me as rather a non issue. The game was desgined with no individual
card limit and a maximum deck size. Many other games are designed with a card
limit and a minimum deck size. It goes with the mechanics. With a NCL, if there
were no deck size maximum, you would never have to worry about running out of
cards, and this is something that the designers apparently wanted us to worry
about. With no maximum deck size, I'd, in a second (well, in theory--I find
decks that size very unweildy), take my 90 card Rush deck, build an identical
second one, and shuffle them together--that way I would never have to worry
about running out of cards, and the built in disadvantage of using a high
cycle, card intensive deck goes away.

>>It really is a joke this, you know.>>

I fail to see how it is any more of a joke that Magic's 60 card minimum, Xena's
40 card maximum, or Pok-e-man's 60 card total deck limit. It is part of the
built in mechanics of the game.

>>You guys bang on and on about not having a CL when there is, in fact, a very
rigid limit on the number of cards that you may put in your deck, i.e. 90 in
tournament play.>>

Yup.

>>That's a CL that Shadowfist doesn't have and it's great. My last
tournament-winning deck had 196 cards in it and is lots of fun to play
in consequence.>>

And I am always rather annoyed by people who play any game with decks that are
that big. It is a pain in the ass sitting around waiting for them to shuffle,
it never gets shuffled adaquately, and the decks are always falling over.
Everyone likes different stuff.

>>This lack of a deck limit means that, unlike VTES,
there is a genuinely infinite number of decks that you can construct.
VTES supposed variety seems like a straight-jacket by comparison.>>

Yeah, I suppose if you want to look at it like that. Yet CL VTES's supposed
variety seems like a straight-jacket by comparison to decks made under the
regular rules.

Messages.Author: Joshua Duffin

Andrew S. Davidson <a...@csi.com> wrote in message news:<1F186CE489BFFCDA.F70CCE67...@lp.airnews.net>...

> On 27 Jun 2001 13:23:58 -0700, Joshua Duffin wrote:
>
> >In general, card limits in CCGs are an attempt to limit the effect of
> >broken cards. Games that don't have broken cards don't need a CL.
> >Shadowfist has been played - in fact I think you've even done it, if
> >I remember right - without using its official 5CL and found to be
> >fairly balanced even without limits. Likewise, VTES doesn't need a
> >limit to be balanced. So why impose one on it?
>
> Apart from setting a ceiling for a play set and eliminating monotonous
> decks, I'd say because the lack of a CL forces you to errata cards
> more frequently. A good example is Wake with Evening's Freshness
> which got an ugly errata. The reason for this was some concern about
> being able to pack large numbers of them which you could freely cycle
> out of your hand. If the game had had a CL then this wouldn't have
> been necessary.

The use of a CL allows you to ignore broken cards, if you so desire,
and just force them to come up less often. But they are every bit
as broken when they show up. Most VTES cards that have had errata
would have been just as bad under 4CL: Return to Innocence, Tomb of
Rameses III, Thoughts Betrayed.

It's true that Wake would probably not be a problem freely cyclable
under a 4CL (or even a 6CL). It's not even much of a problem under
a 90CL. But its cost is insufficient for its effect (under original
Jyhad cardtext) so it got errataed (and reprinted with corrected
wording).

I've seen plenty of monotonous Magic decks, and they've had a 4CL
for years and years. I don't think a CL is any true remedy for
monotony.

> The thing about CCGs is that tournament players are often totally
> ruthless about breaking the game. If there's even the slightest
> weakness in the game system they will push on it until it breaks. I
> know this because I do it myself. A CL provides a safety net for
> stuff that isn't caught in playtest and that's why every single CCG
> apart from VTES has one. That's certainly why Shadowfist has one -
> the designer said so himself. He thought that the game might work
> without one but played it safe. Having thought about it, I'm fairly
> sure that he's wrong and I backed away from running a NCL event. The
> game would work fine for the most part with NCL but that's not good
> enough - players would instantly seize on the parts that weren't fine
> and destroy the game with them.

A CL does sort of provide a safety net, but only if you don't mind
hitting the ground anyway, just not quite as hard. In Shadowfist,
Dangerous Experiment got errataed despite the 5CL, as did Wind on
the Mountain, Vivisector, etc... in Magic, they ended up banning (!)
quite a number of cards after instituting the 4CL, and restricting
others to 1CL...

> Oh, and another thing. If there were a CL then you'd be able to ditch
> the other CL which VTES does have - the limit on deck size. It really
> is a joke this, you know. You guys bang on and on about not having a
> CL when there is, in fact, a very rigid limit on the number of cards
> that you may put in your deck, i.e. 90 in tournament play. That's a
> CL that Shadowfist doesn't have and it's great. My last
> tournament-winning deck had 196 cards in it and is lots of fun to play
> in consequence. This lack of a deck limit means that, unlike VTES,
> there is a genuinely infinite number of decks that you can construct.
> VTES supposed variety seems like a straight-jacket by comparison.

You're right, VTES does have a 90CL for tournaments. I don't see
mega-huge decks as something that would be better than being able
to choose the number of each card I want to play with, though.

> Doomtown takes yet another approach. There is a tight CL of 4 and a
> fixed deck size of 52. But you can recycle your discards and so you
> may draw and play a given card a potentially infinite number of times.
> This is a whole new ball game and has the great merit that you are
> mostly unlikely to run dry as can happen in the other two games.

That's an interesting one.

> Still, there's a lot to be said for VTES taking a different approach
> too - it'd be dull if these CCG had identical mechanics. Just be
> aware that there is a rich universe of possibilities out there and
> there's something to be said for them all.

I'm certainly aware that there are other possibilities, I just don't
think that the low-CL one would be good for VTES.

Josh

Messages.Body:

Empty library? Tricky, but...

7 Cards in hand, 33 cards in your ash heap.

If you play Whispers from the Dead to go get a Summon Soul, say, you
cannot draw up a card (having no cards left in your library. So, you get
the Summon Soul in your hand, but do not have to discard (since you've got
7, not 8 cards as you usually would after playing Whispers.)

If you Summon Soul (Superior), you can go put the Whispers and whatever
card it is you want back into your library. Because of:

"If you hold fewer cards in hand than your hand size because your library is
empty and then one or more cards are returned to your library, immediately
draw the cards into your hand (stopping if your reach your hand size).
[LSJ 20001127]"

you draw up one of the two cards (either, "the card you want," or the
Whispers.) Either way, the Summon Soul is removed from the game.

If you just Whispers "the card you want" out of your ash heap, you've
got it now, but you've got one less Whispers in your hand of 7 cards. You
can follow this iteratively, you can do this no more than 7 times before
your recycling is over.

Whispers is clearly not the way to go for "infinite" cycling.

If you play purely Summon Soul, each time you do it, you'll remove a
Summon Soul from the game. This certainly seems to be the best way, and
while it requires NEC, it's free. Obviously, to keep doing this Ad
Infinitum, you get a Summon Soul for every Summon Soul you play (on average;
you can go get 2 cards "you want" in one Summon, but you need to Summon up 2
more Summon Souls to keep from running out of Summon Souls later on).
Basic trick being: Summon Soul to go get a bleed card and a stealth
card. You draw up either one, but assume (worst case) it's the stealth
card. Summon again to get 2 more Summon Souls, and you draw into the bleed
card, and have 2 Summon Souls in your ash heap.
Then bleed, with your prey knowing full well you've got stealth (if he
had intercept left, he'd be stopping this silly "go get bleed and stealth"
shit =).
If he tries to block, you stealth it through. Lather, rinse, repeat.
If not, you've got stealth left; go get 2 bleed cards instead, so he
sees he'll need to block.

You can do this until your deck runs out of Summon Souls, but you only
need like, 2 bleed cards, and 2 stealth cards; nobody can remove them from
the game. The other 36 Cards can be 28 Summon Souls, 5 Deal with the Devil,
and threes card of your choice (maybe Leonardo, Morgue HG, Tower of London).
You can do the recycling trick, if you have 3 vamps with NEC (crypt of
Isabel, Rudolpho, Andrea, and Carlotta, 3 copies of each) you can
Govern+stealth 14 times for 3 actions a turn, once you're out of library.
(Unless you stop to go get your 3 cards of choice, which you maybe should.
Hm. Maybe 2 Minion Taps in there, so you can get Carlotta or Andrea
down to one blood, and Summon Soul (at inferior, keeping the card in the
game) 3 times either/each while you're Dealing with the Devil?

Cute. Certianly MUCH more viable (and easier to get the Summon Souls!)
in a 40 card version, I think. Looks like fun!

--
Pat Ricochet
Soul Jar'rn Fool of Atlanta

Messages.Author: Vince Johnson
Messages.Body:
Magic's brokenness was a result of limits and cards too powerful no matter
how many you had.

I used to believe Jyhad needed limits, but now I don't think so. I know
I've only been back a short while, but in what I've seen, especially of
emergent decks. Limits are a waste of time as many decks now contain
several variations of cards (example Forced Awakening and WwEF are often
mixed in one deck for their abilities). Limits kill the fun in theme decks
which are in turn dealt with in often simple ways. Also, no card in Jyhad
is really too powerful. But what is awkward is that it was mostly in the
Ancient Hearts set where most of the "powerful" cards existed, the set seen
very little in player hands. Now these cards are reprinted in some cases
and in others obsolete.

Jyhad is a fun game. It has complexity in it's simplicity, story in it's
gameplay, a theme many people are interested, and has been around longer
than most card games in existence without the flood of excess cards (see the
looming demise of Pokemon and Magic)

Vince

Messages.Author: Jacob
Messages.Body:
Where I play, we regulary use 4CL. and no limit to the deck. It makes the game
longer. and more variations. It is normal to reley on 4 to 7 different
diciplines in a deck. and the normal deck is around 200 cards.
I do beleave that no CL makes V:TEs more like magic, making a deck that's only
able to do one thing. If there is a 4CL, you can not make a deck relying on
S:CE because there isen't that many S:CE cards. you have to come up with some
other way to help your vanpiers to get beaten up. We also get to use the more
opscure cards, that people don't use in no CL..
I played the other day against a Tremere Assimite deck, it was around 300
cards, using Auspex, Celerety, Dominate, fortitude, Obfuscate, Quietus,
Thaumaturgy. And it was very effective, It could do everything.
If there should be a vote for no CL or 4CL I would vote for 4CL. Makes the game
better. The only thing I can come up why there shoud be no CL is the games with
we play with 4CL takes about 4-6 hours 4 players. But then again I like that.

Jacob

Messages.Author: Emmit Svenson
Messages.Body:
vte...@white-wolf.com (LSJ) wrote in message news:<9hqhgg$d4d$1...@taliesin.netcom.net.uk>...

> Visit from the Capuchin doesn't help burn through your library.
> It just allows you to treat the top X of your deck as part of
> your hand. Try Deal with the Devil, The Barrens, or Fragment of the
> Book of Nod instead.

Sorry, I should have clarified.

Typical turn with this deck once the 40-card library is exhausted (2
copies of VftC are needed.):

Untap.

Play Visit from the Capuchin.

Use Potchli/Sargon Fragment to recycle a 3-card combo.
(Govern/Seduction/Call Hungry, for example)

Play the combo. (With your laptop/Tasha/Simmons bleeder, perhaps.)

Use Waste Management to recycle Visit from the Capuchin.

This allows you to hold 6 appropriate defense cards (Wakes,
Deflections, Spiritual Interventions, Obediences, Pulling Strings,
etc., depending on your predator) between turns. When you run low on
defensive cards, replace them from the ash heap instead of Visit from
the Capuchin.

You're right: Deal with the Devil, Fragment and Barrens are better for
exhausting the library in the first place. But Dreams of the Sphinx is
a must!

won't notice the difference of not having 12 majesties. I resisted
going to NCL really, but when I looked at the effective CL decks we had
in our group I realized they really weren't any different than effective
NCL decks you could find on the internet. For the same reason as S:CE
above, you can have 20 stealth cards and 20 bleed modifiers in a deck
without going over 4 of each. In fact, with as many expansions out as

bleed... which was the main reason I was convinced to go to NCL. I
don't like stealth bleed.

you have to come up with some

> opscure cards, that people don't use in no CL..

Ironically, I find i use a lot more different cards now as I can build a
combo around a certain card and expect to get the cards for that combo.
For example, I might actually play with cryptic mission, corruption, or
Tremere in general since I know I will be able to get cards that support

> cards, using Auspex, Celerety, Dominate, fortitude, Obfuscate, Quietus,

2-3 disciplines is a lot more likely the culprit for your very long

in NCL play. Most NCL players conform to tournament rules and thus a 90
card deck cap. I could fit a lot more different cards if we were
playing 200 card decks in our play group. (Though I don't think I'd
ever play with that many...)

Tig

Messages.Author: Derek Ray
Messages.Body:
in general, i agree with everything Tig threw out in his post - I have
to tack onto this one bit, though.

On Tue, 03 Jul 2001 11:18:28 -0700, TigToad <tig...@qwest.net> wrote:

>> I played the other day against a Tremere Assimite deck, it was around 300
>> cards, using Auspex, Celerety, Dominate, fortitude, Obfuscate, Quietus,
>> Thaumaturgy. And it was very effective, It could do everything.

...But I'll bet it took 3 turns to actually make anything happen,
explaining the 6-hour game problem. I do not consider decks that take
3 turns to complete one tactic "effective".

>I think the fact you are playing with 200-300 card decks using more than
>2-3 disciplines is a lot more likely the culprit for your very long
>games and your use of lots and lots of different cards than what you see

When your only available actions are either "bleed for 1", or actions
that do nothing to help you oust your prey, then your games will tend
to take longer. I sat cross-table from an intercept deck last night,
and we spent a great number of actions and blocks trading his Rack
back and forth between us. Both of us could really have used it, but
when you get right down to it, those were completely wasted actions
and combats on both our parts, and did nothing but set up our
respective preys and prolong the game.

Card limit play taken to the above extreme simply reinforces that
problem by encouraging non-useful actions (as they're the only ones in
your hand).

>in NCL play. Most NCL players conform to tournament rules and thus a 90
>card deck cap. I could fit a lot more different cards if we were
>playing 200 card decks in our play group. (Though I don't think I'd
>ever play with that many...)

I cannot imagine a 300 card deck, played under 4CL, that could
actually accomplish anything with any degree of consistency, or that
could even conduct simple actions with any hope of having them happen.
Assuming the above Tremere/Assamite deck, there are (more or less) six
different disciplines to draw from: DOM/THA/AUS and QUI/CEL/OBF.

A quickly filtered search reveals that there are approximately 22
distinct cards for each discipline -- meaning that under a 4CL, a
six-discipline deck could conceivably have 528 cards. Insane. A
further run-by notes that with a 7-card hand and a 300-card deck, your
"window" onto your strategy is approximately one-fifth of one percent;
specifically, 0.23%. Draw your own conclusions.

-- Derek

Of course, Malkavian stealth-bleed is helped by no card limits
as much as any other deck. At least you make a token effort at
limiting which +stealth and +bleed cards they have at their
disposal with a card limit. The problem with this deck isnt
the card limit or deck size limit... its the fact that it is
the optimal method of winning the game. It goes directly to
the most fundamental aspect of the game requiring almost no
special cards or combos... it is, in all card games, one of the
defining examples of the term "broken".

Which is not to say it is unbeatable with enough players at
the table all working against it or that the game in a general
sense is not worth playing. It just needs to be reigned in
a bit...

>It might well enhance the social experience of playing V:TES. It makes
>games go on a long time, you get to see lots of different cards played,
>it's very hard to oust someone quickly (and so spoil their fun) and
>usually any given card you get into play will stick around for a few
>turns so you get to "play" with it a bit more.

These are all things people will probably like. Liking things
in a game usually means you want them there. :)

>But it's no longer a competitive game of skill.

Ah! Well, here you are making a subjective value judgement.
Also known as an opinion. Not worth very much in the scheme
of things.

I personally have no stake in a card limit or not... I do know the
game fairly well, however, and a card limit would mean that a player
would have to seek out and use a greater variety of cards. This means

Messages.Author: Scott DiBerardino
Messages.Body:
Many times over the years, I've seen the 4CL and NL camps go at each other
with argument and counter-argument, rhetoric and counter-rhetoric. I've read
the diatribes, the essays, the maths.

Here's my experience.

I played the game fairly extensively when it first came out. We had adopted
a card limit on Magic *before* the tournament rules, mainly as a way to
balance suitcases against people with a couple starters. It seemed natural
to do the same for Jyhad. Again, not because of the game design, but because
of social pressures brought on by different levels of investment in the
group. "Right" or "wrong" it's what we all decided to do.

We had a good time. Games usually lasted a long time, we added a lot of
role-playing atmosphere. We generally discouraged Malk stealth-bleed because
it was seen as "cheap" and "no fun".

We stopped playing after awhile because there was always something new to
try, and people moved away, and people got tired of CCG money-pits.

A couple years later (maybe after Sabbat), a new group started playing
again. I had read the arguments, the diatribes. We tried out No Limits.

After about a half-dozen boring boring games, we quietly retired Jyhad for
good.

It wasn't because of Malkavian stealth-bleed. It wasn't because of broken
cards from expansions. It wasn't because of poor players.

It was deadly boring.

As an example, one guy had a Brujah weenie deck with Computer Hacking,
Flash, and Thrown Sewer Lid and not much else. Win or lose, he was extremely
boring to play against. Most other decks brought to the table were along
these lines, so focused as to provoke lethargy.

I believe that Card Limits *do* break the game in subtle but limited ways.
No Limits breaks the game (for me!) in one unavoidable huge way - it was no
longer fun to play.

And the holier-than-thou attitude on the No Limits side certainly doesn't
help their arguments. No one is convinced when they are insulted.

And if you're curious, the only way we play now is with pre-constructed
decks - the eight released by White Wolf, plus seven for the original clans
I put together out of a large set of original Jyhad.

And we're having fun again.

-scott \\ sdib...@student.umass.edu

-- Dan Quisenberry

Acting player: You have blocked my computer hacking! We go to combat. Anything

Blocking player: (long sigh) Nooooo.....

Lid.

> No Limits breaks the game (for me!) in one unavoidable huge way - it was no

that for you. But everyone has their tastes, I guess.

> And the holier-than-thou attitude on the No Limits side certainly doesn't
> help their arguments. No one is convinced when they are insulted.

I don't think anyone really means to be arrogant about the superiority of NCL.
It's just that when you see the same arguments over and over about NCL that seem
to have a limited perspective and not be very well thought out you, eventually
start to classify its adherents into the same box whether they belong there or
not. The population on this newsgroup has encountered over and over new people
coming in who have played something like 4CL in their local playgroups, who damn
NCL but have never really tried it, and seem to always do so for the same reasons
that most here have found to be invalid when examined. So it's kind of natural to
slap your head every time it happens and often let impatience get the better of you
as you try to explain to the new person that it's all been said before and they're
not telling you anything new however much they think they are and you're pretty
sure it's wrong. No doubt that sounds like arrogance. In truth, it's more a form
of irritable weariness.

> decks - the eight released by White Wolf, plus seven for the original clans
> I put together out of a large set of original Jyhad.
>

then it's hard to fathom why you would enjoy players playing the same decks over and over
even if they're not focused on a relatively small number of cards. But whatever works
for you is cool. I am glad you're finding happiness with game, though. In whatever form
works for you.

Fred

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <B7688F1B.1F9CC%sdib...@student.umass.edu>, Scott
DiBerardino <sdib...@student.umass.edu> writes

>And the holier-than-thou attitude on the No Limits side certainly doesn't
>help their arguments. No one is convinced when they are insulted.

The problem is this:

In general, the xCL factions[0] tend to:

1) Believe that they are right, come what may. No argument can ever be
remotely convincing.

2) Have to convince themselves they are right, especially because they
are playing with a non-official set of rules. Often loudly.

3) In general, those arguing for xCL have tended to be weaker
argumentatively. This is not an indictment of xCL players generally,

just a general feeling of those players who have argued for it. If
someone coherent were to argue for it, they'd do a lot better.

4) They never/rarely encounter all the inherent limits in the game,
repeat-wise, because they are running xCL. Thus they argue how NL
would be broken, not understanding its self-righting mechanism.

5) Because they can't ever stack up on a certain form of defence, they
don't understand just how easy it is to defend against "boring" decks

- all you need is access to *one* source of damage prevention, and
you can load up on it to save your ass etc. against that boring
Brujah deck, from your example. (Or Combat Ends, or Dodge, or
whatever.)

6) Ignore the fact that, from the ground up, Jyhad was designed to have
no card limits. Granted, designer intent is not an argument winner,
but it is highly persuasive when viewed with all the rules and card
texts that actively work to support it.

7) Go on about abusive combos (or some similar facet they dislike),
telling us how xCL balances them - when, in fact, it just makes them
less likely (since I only have four Killer Bleed Cards in my deck)
and harder to defend against (since I can't have that bleed bounce I
want)

8) Tell us how it favours the new player when Jyhad, again, doesn't work

for the vast majority of cards (with only half a dozen exceptions)
having more power when they're less common. Awe is not more powerful

than Bewitching Oration. Raven Spy is not more powerful than Cat's
Guidance. Were this first edition Magic - where a Black Lotus was
more powerful than a comparative common/land card - it'd be a valid
comparison. But Jyhad was designed with a very strong cost->effect
ethic. Compare, say, Dominate cards such as Govern the Unaligned
against Dominate Kine. The latter isn't more powerful than the
former just because it is less common. And then you lose the ability

to use all the nice common cards you've collected - which are
perfectly playable. So the newbie player can play 4 Bewitching
Orations and 1 Awe, maybe, whereas the old suitcase guy can play 4 of

each. The newbie could benefit from being able to put 7 Bewitching
Orations in because the card is good and powerful in itself, and easy

to get hold of because it's common.

9) Fail to understand that, as a result of Jyhad's limited card pool (as

it has been for a very, very long time) and comparitively huge
numbers of clans and disciplines, the amount of redundancy is
limited. Again, taking Magic as the counter-example - with five
colours and no "clan" concept really[1], it's very easy to load up 40

cards into red, 40 into blue etc. and find that, at the end of the
day, red actually has quite a few very similar cards which, whilst
not identical, can do good impersonations of one another. Once you
leave stealth, bleed and intercept alone, the amount of redundancy in

cards in V:TES is very limited - again, an inherent design decision,
because they knew people could and would buy lots of cards (Magic had

taught them this), so why not do things a bit differently?

10) Which leads us on to the fact that Jyhad has clearly been designed
at numerous points to work well with decks focussed around one card
strategies/tactics (split the difference between the two as you like,

obviously). Corruption, from Ancient Hearts, was one extreme
(obviously) example of such a card - with only x (4 or 6) in a deck,
it's utterly pointless. But there are many cards which you can focus

a deck strategy/tactic around which you can't use properly if there
are only one or two of them. Frex, the various Invitation Accepted
variants. If you want a Cammy clan so you can do PS etc., you need
to be able to "guarantee" the Join-Camarilla vote comes up quickly.
This is a facet of 9), given the general lack of redundancy in many
areas.

And when you sit down and explain all these things - and many more
besides - you most often get incoherent abuse back. As has been pointed
out, people are quite welcome to play "Snap" with their Jyhad cards, but
most would prefer (IMHO etc.) that we didn't get abused because we
choose to play the real game with them.

[0] Obviously, there are people out there playing xCL who are doing none
of these things. The vast majority, however, of those who argue for xCL
online tend to end up like this.

[1] Creature type, I guess, but they're not quite as intrinsic as the
clan nature of Vampire.



Messages.Author: Wes
Messages.Body:
"James Coupe" <ja...@zephyr.org.uk> wrote

<snip excellent points>

Might I also add that NCL includes XCL as a subset? This may sound basic but
it's something many don't seem to consider.

Many of my decks are able to be played in a 4CL environment. I think most of
the pre-constructed in both Sabbat War and Final Nights are 4CL-compliant,
and they aren't *that* bad...

Players that include multiple copies of one card often pay for their focus
when going up against a deck which is its nemesis. Sometimes, diversity will
make a deck more robust. Sometimes it won't. This is where your skill in
designing decks comes in. It seems to me that there would be very little
'thought' going into a 300-card deck under 4CL. How could there be?

My initial playgroup played under 4CL because we incorrectly assumed that
there was a limit (not sure why really--none of us played Magic). When we
found out there wasn't a card limit, we stopped playing that way.

Of course, I have no problem with people playing under their own
house-rules, but you *have* to recognize that your house rule is not and
*should not* be a rule that is applied to the game in general.

When I play Chess, I won't let someone claim that 'En Passant' isn't a valid
move, because they have never heard of it. The rules are the rules.
Disallowing a rule changes the nature of the game. Either play Chess or
don't. Either play Jyhad or don't. But be sure you realize that under 4CL,
you are *not* playing Jyhad as it is meant to be.

And for god's sake, don't show up at a tournament thinking that 4CL is
enforced... I hate that.

Cheers,
WES

>of NCL versus xCL, but asserted that Vampire was no fun for my group in an
>NCL environment.

In your group, I would simply build decks that defeated the
one-trick-pony decks without being excessively "boring" or visibly
one-tricky.

It's often worth noting that a deck that can do nothing but one thing
is usually vulnerable to good play even if your deck is NOT designed
to beat it -- a Brujah thrown-objects deck, for example, can get into
combat lots with Bum's Rush. But it can't bleed for more than 1, and
it tends not to win as a result due to its fragility. If one includes
Legal Manipulations, one loses the ability to constantly get into
combat, and one becomes vulnerable to Deflections.

In other words, try not blocking it, even if it DOES bleed for 3.
Eventually you'll be able to point out to the guy that he's NOT
WINNING. If you are playing with people whose goal is not "to win",
then the people you play with are the problem, not the game itself,
and there's nothing to be done about it.

Most people want to win.

>I heard an anecdote recently about a player I knew who encountered "the game
>designers" (presumably post-Garfield WotC types). They were shocked that she
>was used to 4-hour marathon games with slow development; they had designed
>and always played the game as a 90-minute brawl.
>
>Back in the day, I liked the 4-hour marathon better than the 90-minute
>brawl.

Unfortunately, you are in the (vast) minority. The general
population, which is our ONLY source of new players, likes games to be
at least REASONABLY quick. This is one of V:TES's big weaknesses; the
sheer length of the game means that a great amount of time needs to be
set aside to play, and a quick loss "feels" worse than it would in a
60-minute game.

Many/most current V:TES players do like the "marathon" games. But
without new blood, the game will die -- which the original designers
appear to have known well, from your anecdote above. Very few people
want to learn a game that's going to chop out huge amounts of their
time; it simply doesn't fit in today's society.

NCL decks -do- decrease game length; whether or not they are
effective, they do one thing and do it well, and the person playing
them generally is completely prepared for anything their own deck will
do. Strategic decisions come quicker, combat moves more rapidly, etc.
This is NOT a bad thing.

xCL decks and toolboxes tend to INCREASE game length; strategic
decisions are much more difficult, many different interactions arise,
and as a result players take a lot longer to make their turns. This
is not, in itself, a bad thing either.... but it is going to turn new
players off. Gratuitously banning NL decks is a self-limiting
proposition.

You have to separate ability from choice of strategy. Just because the guy didn't

>This only works in the context of serial games.

Not necessarily.

A toolboxed deck works very efficiently against such. If you have just
enough defence to fend them off so that you can get by, you can control
the game. If you view Jyhad as a big circle of rock-paper-scissors -
which it can be, viewed at an abstract enough level - if you have a
small piece of paper, you can stop that rock for five seconds, just
enough to allow your scissors to go off.

The function of the metagame is also an important one, but it is not the
*only* important one. A focussed deck, which needs to change the
defence it mounts each time, either requires a skillful player - one
with great talent for creative play, lateral thinking and diplomacy - or
would benefit from some tool-boxing.

For those reading this in .misc, the general definitions of toolbox and
metagame so far as .jyhad is concerned might be:

Toolbox - to have a deck, still capable of winning, but which does not
have complete focus on one strategy. An analogous situation in Magic
might be a deck with 10 Mountains, 3 Plains, 3 Islands, 2 Swamps and a
Forest - such that it can still have a balance in favour of damage from
the mountains etc., but is capable of dealing with other plans as
necessary.

Metagame - the function by which players adapt to those around them,
following other games.

>And, if I were to prepare
>defenses for every possible OTP, my deck would become ineffective anyway.

Not true. The toolbox archetype has been shown to be very effective
though not, of course, to everyone's taste.

The key is working out how you can defend across a broad range of items
without becoming so weak that you can't defend against the important
ones properly.

http://www.thelasombra.com/decks/twd.htm#rob2 is an excellent example of
such. It does, however, require a high level of skill to pull off
properly.

8 commons, 3 uncommons, 1 rare. (Picking random numbers from the air.)

The deck wanting lots of Strike: Combat Ends allows itself 8 Majesties

I could get Immortal Grapple as Uncommon (Sabbat), but that still only

but not intended as abuse in any way, shape or form.

>I heard an anecdote recently about a player I knew who encountered "the game
>designers" (presumably post-Garfield WotC types).

This is not an anecdote in the Urban Legend style and comes from
Garfield himself. The White Wolf guide (my copy of which I have lost, I
will see if Amazon have any at some point, or something) that came out a
number of years ago had a preface from Garfield which makes for some of
the most profound and exciting writing ever found on Jyhad.

This was, however, as I recall found during the development cycle -
rather than afterwards. Constructs such as the Edge and, I'm not sure
on this one, the pool for ousting were counter-acting agents to this.

> They were shocked that she
>was used to 4-hour marathon games with slow development; they had designed
>and always played the game as a 90-minute brawl.
>
>Back in the day, I liked the 4-hour marathon better than the 90-minute
>brawl.

Many people prefer the 4 hour marathon. Final rounds of tournaments,
for instance, habitually effectively untimed. (Allowable under the
V:EKN tournament rules.) Jyhad is supposed to be a game of slow
development and intrigue.

The difference between 90 minute brawls and 4 hour marathons is not one
of xCL vs NL, however. Someone wanting to turn a game into a 90 minute
brawl stands a very good chance of doing so (and possibly invoking the
wrath of all other players, who may have somewhat slower strategies)
whether under xCL or NL. Indeed, the fact that the S&B archetype is
increased in relative power under xCL might make it substantially
*easier* to turn an xCL game into a brawl. However, that's a different
matter.

The main defining factor of brawl or marathon is play-style of players,
rather than play-style enforced by the rules, so far as I have ever been
aware.

I don't mind either really, though the 4-hour ones seem rarer now that our
decks are more competitive. Winning generally equates to being the fastest
deck at the table. The longest game I remember in recent times is about 2
1/2 hours. Most of ours fall under 1 1/2 or even 1 hour I would guess. I
played five different decks last Sunday between 11am and 5pm if that tells
you anything...

However, I do have fond memories of those marathon games... I wonder if
there would be some way to establish the makings of a long game without
imposing card limits. Maybe a period of 'ceasefire' for a certain amount of
turns or something. Unlimited deck-sizes would help here. Playing with only
Jyhad starters and a few boosters might do the job. I recall that the Final
Nights pre-release games were a bit longer than usual.

I do wonder however how much fun your games can be when there is absolutely
no variation. Using only the pre-constructed decks seems to me to be more
boring than the Potence-pitch deck you described earlier. Designing decks is
the aspect of the game that I enjoy the most. However, even when I have
created a successful deck, I usually retire it so I can have fun building
another. Surely, your group must be missing out... on this aspect if nothing
else.

In my experience, the players who give up on Jyhad are not the ones who lose
the most, but on those who create the least. Or, possibly moreso, those who
play *against* those who create the least, ie. with a very limited number of
decks. Several of our players have one deck which they play with (which they
*did* construct, granted) and only occasionally do they try to build
another. It's boring as hell for everyone involved.

This is also probably why Malkavian S&B still have a bad name... nobody
wanted to face them because they were so common and lacking in originality.
I have to admit that I still groan every time I see one. Unless the deck is
a new or interesting spin on Malkavians, I'm just not that intrigued. So
when Noal pulled out Gilbert Duane on Sunday, I frowned... when he started
calling votes, I became interested.

Personally, I'd much rather win a game with something new and interesting
than with something old and proven, but that's just me.

Cost in hand for strategy. Opportunity cost of passing vote.

(These costs may be near-negligible but V:TES's constant replace
mechanism - such that a card in the hand is denying you other cards
rather than a regular replace mechanism - and similar things all play a
vitally significant role in the game, at a fundamental level, so
fundamental that they can be over-looked if you're not careful.)

> (Of course, Arika, Kindred Coercion and,
>Elder Kindred Network add up to 20-some pool worth of hurt...)

The more common, and simpler, Delaying Tactics leaves you with an empty
vampire. (Until Final Nights finally got round to editing Banishment,
I'd have also snickered and Banished Anneke with Igo. Or something.)

To pull the scenario you detail off, you need a specific, though not
impossible or even improbable, set of occurrences.

You cannot, for instance, get 4 votes from Awe for free, as you can with
. You have to spend at least 2 blood (superior), and the opportunity
cost of Voter Cap, whilst potentially small, is not insignificant. If
you start becoming abusive with Voter Cap, a lot of people on tables
will start turning round and abusing you repeatedly, refusing to aid
your votes, blocking them, rushing your vampires cross-table (a worried
grand-predator, for instance) in order to bring you back under control -
such that loading up on Voter Captivation will have significant
downsides; you'll either have to discard them (thus alerting people to
"He's got billions!"), play them (such that you start looking very
threatening with that extra 6 pool you just got back this turn with
three votes), allow them to jam your hand etc. Voter Captivation is a
very good card, but is inherently limitable.

V:TES, as I hope the above demonstrates, is very, very clearly oriented
to cost->effect, where cost can include:

- deck slot (90 card maximum, under tournament rules)
- hand slot (denying you seeing the card its replacing)
- opportunity cost (how often can you play it - Bewitching Oration is
fucked if you never get a vote passed that damn !Ventrue deck)
- pool/blood cost (depleting your resources)
- minion cost (using a minion card i.e. non-master card, requires a
minion to do it - unlike, taking Magic again[0], the fact that you can

use a Fireball whether you've got a Serrated Dangle out or not)
- discipline/clan requirement (possibly onerous, depending on your deck)

etc. etc. etc.

With very, very few exceptions (mostly found in Ancient Hearts, namely
Tomb and Return to Innocence, IMHO), rarity has never been a factor for
finding "better" cards. The fundamental, powerful basic cards for any
strategy can be found at common usually - even if, for your purposes, a
rare card might be "better". (Like if I want to steal a location on a
bleed card as another function, I'm screwed if all I have is Govern the
Unaligned instead of Dominate Kine - that doesn't make GtA less
powerful, just it has a different function, and that three pool gain
potentially is powerful enough in itself.)

Take bleed:

- Govern the Unaligned
- Legal Manipulations
- Laptop Computer
- Conditioning/Bonding/Threats

Take combat defence:

- Majesty
- Skin of Rock
- Dodge
- Fake Out
- Flash

Take vote:

- Conservative Agitation
- Kine Resources Contested
- Autarkis Persecution
- Bewitching Oration
- Bribes
- Disputed Territory

Stealth:

- Lost in Crowds
- Faceless Night
- Cloak the Gathering

Generically Useful Master Cards:

- Blood Doll
- Minion Tap
- The Barrens
- Elder Library (not my cup of tea, but some people have a thing for it
and in large combo decks, it's useful because of the extra sight)
- Ascendance/Short Term Investment/Protracted Investment (we'll have a
flame war along in a minute about the relative minutes, trust me)

Defence/Reaction:

- Enhanced Senses
- The Spirit's Touch
- Telepathic Counter
- Telepathic Misdirection
- Wake with Evening's Freshness (with a mild fix, now)
- Deflection

and so on.

A **lot** of key cards can be found at common level. The major flaw
here is offensive combat. The designers appear to have been, from
Garfield's writings, very combat heavy in their environment - attack,
rather than defence. The line was something like: "We often fought over
whether the Gangrel or Brujah were the better combat clan. In the end,
we decided on the Gangrel - after all, the Brujah do have Presence."
(Words to that effect, but I don't have the book anymore) Presence, it
turned out, was the exact counter to combat - because no-one ever
envisaged quite how powerful Strike: Combat Ends would be in the scheme
of things and, try as we might, some things get passed over in
play-testing. So, Immortal Grapple was the one flaw - if you wanted to
go on the offensive combat wise, IG turned out to be fairly essential.
Again, a lot of commons are around - Bum's Rush, Undead Strength, Wolf
Claws etc. But IG just turned out be necessary because potential abuses
of Presence (well, Strike: Combat Ends really, but it's all you sleazy
Presence mongers in reality - we know who you are) were possible.

However, for n00bs, there are still dozens of decks that can be
constructed from large numbers of commons with half a dozen uncommons or
rares tossed in if you have them and think they might be useful.

Cost->Power. And common things have a cost and, consequently, power.
Those who positively *need* uncommons, vampire commonality library cards
or rares to compete are missing something. If I don't have pen and
paper, I don't decide to write my life story. If I don't have lots of
Betrayers to make the Betrayer deck (well, and a complete set of all
vampires, too) I can't build that - just because I don't have the cards
and the Betrayer deck isn't inherently unstoppable because it's hard to
make, far from it. So commons are good and useful and powerful and
everyone agrees and we get perfect umma in the group.

Maybe.

[0] Sorry to keep doing this, but V:TES was, in fact, based loosely on
some bits of Magic terminology etc., taking the game in other, very
different directions. It's also the game that most people know a little
about whereas my picking, say, Star Trek is likely to miss a larger
group of people. <troll> Well, that and the Star Trek card game
suckethed mightily when it came out. </troll>

It would be partly being unfamiliar with the new cards, agreed... but moreso
I think it was because of a lack of control or cohesion in the pre-con
decks. The decks were designed well enough, but they were not designed by
the player using them, which made it much harder to judge what should be
done. Some combos are obvious of course but not always. I experienced
hand-jam all day... even after I recognized what the new cards were all
about.

I played the Giovanni deck and ended up taking out all my Potence cards
after the first game because I wanted to have a tighter deck. It worked for
me as my deck became a lot faster and a lot more cohesive. (Not sure if
'cohesive' is the right word here, but I think you will know what I mean).

For making games longer, I suppose adding more pool to start with would
work. 30 pool is just right for something like a tournament, but for a game
which everyone agrees should be long and drawn out, maybe 40 would be
better. Not so much because it provides more 'stuff' but because you are
less vulnerable while you are establishing your controlled region. Of
course, this means the game stops being Jyhad and starts being something
else, but fuck it... whatever works for you.

You might also want to consider building all the decks according to the
Happy Families formula. By doing this, you are automatically including four
disciplines (well, I use it with three, but apply as desired) and the decks
end up slightly less focused but much more robust, in my experience. If
everyone agreed to follow the formula exactly as it is, you might find that
the games are closer to the ideal we are talking about. If *you* are the one
building all the decks, this should be easy enough.

absolutely

fifteen

> Shadowfist, and look for a different experience from Jyhad now.

I can't build a Shadowfist deck to save my life, personally... they all
crash and burn.

The other problem with Jyhad, and in this I am more guilty than most, is
that one player comes up with a cool concept but never gets to play it
properly because his predator runs over him with a focused competitive deck.
I've seen players come up with great ideas but are afraid to play them
against the standard decks around here. It's a shame really... though when
all is said and done, if my prey is taking his sweet time establishing
himself, I'm going to do my best to take advantage of this.

The 'slow' game-variant we are referring to would of course be ideal for
this kind of deck.
