DiBerardino <sdib...@student.umass.edu> writes

>> If you can Google up half a dozen IDs for threads, I'll happily re-post
>> a start article and then respond to it.
>
>Frankly, I don't care that much. I'm not really interested in defending xCL.

If you're going to tell us that there are coherent defences that have
been made and then not spend five minutes digging them up (something I
can't do, since I have no idea what you find to be coherent, persuasive
and convincing), there's nothing I can do. I find it inherently
saddening that you believe there are convincing coherent arguments we
have missed but will do nothing to allow us to see them.

>> A toolboxed deck works very efficiently against such. If you have just
>> enough defence to fend them off so that you can get by, you can control
>> the game. If you view Jyhad as a big circle of rock-paper-scissors -
>> which it can be, viewed at an abstract enough level - if you have a
>> small piece of paper, you can stop that rock for five seconds, just
>> enough to allow your scissors to go off.
>
>I guess my argument reduces to "I don't like playing rock/paper/scissors".
>Or rather, it's more fun when everybody has rock and paper and scissors
>available during the game (and not just between games, like the Jyhad
>metagame does.)

Quantifying "fun" is, of course, a killer, and you can turn a deck into
rock whether you play with xCL or NL. Whether it is an effective rock -
as other arguments detail - is more difficult to decide.

However, one of the best ways to have rock, paper and scissors available
to you all at once is through the *way* you play, not *what* you play.

A Brujah weenie potence combat deck. I rush! I rush again!
Kill! Kill! Destroy!

That's our archetypal rock, for argument's sake.

It's efficient, it's focussed, it can kill a lot of vampires, played
effectively. But let's make stealth and bleed our paper, it coming to
smother our rock with its large bleeds.

The rush deck is rock, not scissors. So it can't ever possibly defend
against the paper. Except it can, through intelligent, efficient play,
through well-aimed rushes, fending its predator off without demolishing
it, through table diplomacy ("Look, you've just Revelationed your
predator, he's got Temptation of Greater Power. If you don't bleed me
with that Arika you have there, I'll go and torporise that Justicared
copy of Tiberius so he can't play it. Deal?"), through intelligent deck
construction.

An intelligent player can turn any deck into rock, paper or scissors, as
and when he needs it. A toolbox player has certain facets at his
disposal (that he has certain powerful cards available, which he can't
necessarily rely on) whereas the focused player have other facets (the
reliability of knowing that she can reliably pull this off, if she can
target it properly) at her disposal.

A player with less play-skill-intelligence, with mono-maniacal
tendencies, can turn any swiss-army knife into a rock.

xCL doesn't stop you making a focused combat deck. It doesn't stop you
making a focused political deck. It doesn't stop you making a focused
bleed deck - the three major deck archetypes from the games inception,
with certain other deck types establishing themselves later. It may,
however, make them less effective, possibly neutering them relatively
speaking.

>>> And, if I were to prepare
>>> defenses for every possible OTP, my deck would become ineffective anyway.
>>
>> Not true. The toolbox archetype has been shown to be very effective
>> though not, of course, to everyone's taste.
>>
>> The key is working out how you can defend across a broad range of items
>> without becoming so weak that you can't defend against the important
>> ones properly.
>>
>> http://www.thelasombra.com/decks/twd.htm#rob2 is an excellent example of
>> such. It does, however, require a high level of skill to pull off
>> properly.
>
>Isn't it a problem of the game that a unfocused design with adequate defense
>is only in the province of "a high level of skill"?

Not from where I stand.

"Unfocused" design requires intelligent discarding, table manipulation,
diplomacy, skill, time and so on to play well. This can provide an
exceptionally powerful deck.

"Focused" design requires certain other facets, all equally intelligent.

Players lacking skill will fall over, the vast majority of the time,
regardless of the deck they play. And the skill needed to play a
toolbox efficiently is different to, rather than inherently better than,
the skill required to play a focused deck well. It appears to be less
common, as many players initially equate NL ==
focused/repetitive/whatever and then find they like that play style.

Focused, one-trick pony decks do not just "win". Intelligent, planned,
carefully thought out play is needed to win with them.

I prefer play skill to be paramount or, rather, highly important, with
luck and randomness adding to the challenge, not distracting from the
skill. If I didn't, I wouldn't play strategic games.

>> The deck wanting lots of Strike: Combat Ends allows itself 8 Majesties
>> (common in Jyhad/V:TES), 8 Staredown (common in Sabbat) and 3 Catatonic
>> Fear (Uncommon in Sabbat).
>>
>> I could get Immortal Grapple as Uncommon (Sabbat), but that still only
>> allows me 3.
>
>I'm not sure what you're point is here.

It's an issue of rock vs paper vs scissors.

You have said you want rock vs paper vs scissors to be available to all.

I want to play a Potence based rush deck - a perfectly sensible idea,
one that the game was inherently designed for. (The combat wombat
archetype was coded in from the ground up. The Brujah combat wombat
deck type similar so.)

How do I get through your S:CE with my rush? You have 19 copies of
Strike: Combat Ends available. I have 3 copies of Immortal Grapple.

Since some cards have no (usable in a given circumstance[0])
alternatives available, and since some of the cards are found at less
common levels, you inherently unbalance the system - perhaps not to a
degree you find objectionable. Some xCL players have professed, at
various points, to prefer slight randomness. Personally, I prefer skill
to be substantially more important.

Under NL, you can have as many copies of S:CE as you want, I can have as
many copies of IG (or Psyche!, Dog Pack, Perfect Clarity, Thoughts
Betrayed, Telepathic Tracking etc.) as I want. I can make my scissors
as big as your paper, whereas card limits - especially scaled card
limits where unusual abilities are found at less common levels[1] -
inherently limit my ability to judge my rock:scissors:paper ratio
carefully. And where the foils are rare, the disparity is substantially
increased.

> My point was that scaled limits
>brought a more level playing field to card access for players with different
>collecting abilities.

Certainly it does. However, it's a slightly false argument, in that
access to rares is not the be all and end all of Jyhad - though it is
critical to certain deck designs.

Limiting newbies from being able to utilise their collection effectively
is far, far more damaging than finding that they're up against a Mr
Suitcase using a deck of 90 rares, IMHO.

>This is a social gaming issue,

To be honest, I have always found that solving social gaming issues is
best handled socially, rather than through rules kludges.

If, as we all do, you find someone really, really boring and uninspired
in their deck design, telling them "We're changing the rules because of
*YOU*" is only likely to rub them up the wrong way. If it *doesn't* rub
them up the wrong way then, IME, neither would social interaction - and
social interaction doesn't leave you with a kludged set of rules to deal
with.

>What's Happy Families?

To try out Happy Families with pre-Sabbat War vampires, try

http://www.zephyr.org.uk/happy.htm

(Disclaimer: my shite web-site that I really will do something with at
some point. Maybe.)

The basic concept is this:

If 10 out of my 12 vampires have Animalism then my deck should include a
number of card attuned to that proportion in my deck.

Let's see we add up all the vampires in a deck and find that:

10 have Animalism
9 have Fortitude
9 have Protean
4 have Potence

As the top four most common disciplines they have. 12 vampire crypt.

And a library of 90 cards.

The numbers now work like this:

Number of master cards in deck = 90 x 20% = 18 master cards
Number of minion cards in deck = 72
Number of discipliness cards in deck =
72 x 12 / ( 10 + 9 + 9 + 4 + 12) = 19.64
Number of Animalism cards in deck =
72 x 10 / ( 10 + 9 + 9 + 4 + 12) = 16.64
Number of Fortitude/Protean cards in deck =
72 x 9 / ( 10 + 9 + 9 + 4 + 12) = 14.73 each
Number of Potence cards in deck =
72 x 4 / ( 10 + 9 + 9 + 4 + 12) = 6.55

Giving a total deck of roughly 90 cards, because of rounding errors etc.

You can fudge this for any number of disciplines, of course, but 4 was
considered "best" by Legbiter when he invented it. 3 or 5 are also
good. 2 can be a bit too few, though good for a vote heavy deck, due to
the increased number of disciplineless cards you'll get in a deck.

What this does is gives you ratios of cards *and* forces you to pay
attention to what's in your crypt so you don't wave your arms at the
deck, thinking there's a lot of Presence in it and only finding that, in
fact, only 9 of your vampires have it.

It doesn't replace deck-building, by any means, but it throws it under a
wonderfully critical light.

Messages.Author: Wes
Messages.Body:
"Scott DiBerardino" <sdib...@student.umass.edu> wrote
>
> What's Happy Families?

It's a method invented by Legbiter for constructing decks. Here's the gist
of it, copied from an old post:
====================
Here is a worked example of building a deck using the Happy Families method,
in response to requests from a number of people.

For those who don't know what i'm talking about, Happy Families is a
deck-constructing formula that aims to build a flexible playable deck around
a given
selection of vampires. Usually these will all be vampires of one clan.
Basically you choose the vamps you want to play with, and the library size
you want to use, and then you determine the cards in the library as follows:

20% or so should be master cards

The remaining 80% or so should be minion cards, divided up with respect to
discipline in the following way:

Count the number of vampires in your crypt: Call this number p. Count the
number of vampires with the most common discipline in your deck: call this
number q. Count the number of vampires with the second most common
discipline in your deck: call this number r.
Count the number of vampires with the third most common discipline in your
deck: call this number s.
Count the number of vampires with the fourth most common discipline in your
deck: call this number t.

Now if 80% of your chosen library size is a, then you want

[(p/[p+q+r+s+t]) x a] cards that require no discipline to play
[(q/[p+q+r+s+t]) x a] cards that require the most common discipline to play
[(r/[p+q+r+s+t]) x a] cards that require the second most common discipline
to play
[(s/[p+q+r+s+t]) x a] cards that require the third most common discipline
to play
[(t/[p+q+r+s+t]) x a] cards that require the fourth most common discipline
to play

You can obviously have more or fewer disciplines than 4, in which case you
adjust the formula accordingly, and i do so, below.

i wanted to build a "kagemusha" Nosferatu bash/vote deck from Jyhad cards
only, to "shadow" my favourite tournament deck. This deck therefore was
made from the contents of just under two boxes of Jyhad boosters given to me
by David tatu [we used the rest to build a Brujah bash/bleed deck for
Michael].

CRYPT:
2 Sheldon 9 POT ANI OBF AUS for Justicar
2 Selma 8 POT ani OBF for Prince
2 Chester 7 POT ANI obf for Primogen
2 Sammy 4 pot ani obf
Agrippina 4 pot OBF
Duck 3 pot obf
Koko 2 pot
Dimple 2 obf

There are 12 vampires in this crypt and all 12 can use disciplineless or
Nossie-only cards. 11 can use pot cards, and a different 11 can use obf
cards. 8 can use ani cards. 6 can use for cards. 2 can use aus cards.

12+11+11+8+6+2 = 50.

Now for the library. 20% or so of your library should be master cards -
fewer if you turn over a lot of minion cards in any one turn, more if you
have Anson, the
Parthenon, Death of my Conscience or some other way of unjamming your hand.

For a 90-card library, 20% = 18 masters.

That leaves 72 minion cards.

Happy families tells us that (12/50) x 72 should be cards that require no
discipline to play, ie 18 cards. (11/50) x 72 should be pot cards, and the
same number should be obf cards, ie 15 pot cards and 15 obf cards. (8/50) x
72 should be ani cards, ie 12. (6/50) x 72 should be for cards, ie 9. (2/50)
x 72 should be aus cards, ie 3.

That's how i decided on the proportions, and here is the deck i actually
built:

18 Masters:

5 Minion Tap
[average blood capacity of this crypt is 5 and 7 twelfths, bit big, and
bloat is going to be your best defence against a quick bleed deck] Fame
3 Blood doll
KRCG News Radio
Giant's Blood
Haven Uncovered
Slum HG
Golconda
Temptation of Greater Power [use as a master-phase bleed against your prey,
and if you are lucky it will set you up for a Parity shift, too!].
The Rack
2 Spawning Pool [An underrated card, in my view, especially if you have ANI
and rat's warning. Actually the surprise value of Temptation/GP and spawning
pool is a lot of the reason for their inclusion - tends to put people off
their game if a really unusual card turns up].

18 No Discipline cards:

2 Parity Shift Archon
4 WWEF
Kindred Restructure
2 Nosferatu Justicar
Fifth Tradition
2 Bum's Rush
2 Taste of Vitae
Second Tradition
Bloodhunt
Saturday Night Special [was Patagia, but the advantage is SOOO marginal. As
far as i can see the only good excuse for using Patagia is if you want to
use the RPG launcher or Flamethrower, and even then the IR goggles are
probably better].

I've now changed this card to another 5th tradition, which became available
when michael decided that rake was surplus to requirements in
his Brujah deck and purged all his prince cards too.

i'm playing fast and loose with the formula here, obviously, because a lot
of these cards require that you have a Prince or Justicar. So i'm trusting
the deck to deliver
that, to some extent.

15 Potence
7 Mighty Grapple
3 Thrown Gate
2 Rampage
3 Undead Strength

15 Obfuscate
5 Cloak the Gathering
2 Mask 1K Faces
3 Faceless Night
2 Spying mission
3 Lost in Crowds

12 Animalism
5 Rat's Warning
Army of Rats
2 Raven Spy
4 Cat's Guidance

9 Fortitude
3 Skin of Rock
5 Skin of Steel
Freak Drive

3 Auspex
2 Telepathic Misdirection
Pulse of the Canaille

That's 8 actions, 6 votes, 2 Retainers, 1 Equip [17 card-based reasons to
tap a vampire, if you like]: 16 Action modifiers: 16 Reactions: 23 combat
cards.

Experience shows this is roughly the right proportion of different card
types for a nice flowy kind of deck that is always up to stuff.
==============================

Cheers,
WES

Why is this good? It will certainly "promote" variation - but only in

and tie will "promote" variation. Varied, sure. Justification?

matters. Other card games (with entirely different rules sets, aims,
balancing points, design paradigms, victory conditions, self-righting
mechanisms and so forth) can't do this so, OF COURSE, we shouldn't be
able to either.

selection of Majesty, Staredown, Catatonic Fear and Dodge?

>Other CCGs have to deal with not being able to build a deck
>around a single concept and eveyrone still has fun.

Magic was built around the idea that no deck could ever become really,
really, really focused because no-one would have more than 400 cards
'cos, well, buying that many cards is just plain stupid. The xCL helped
combat this, and the game was/has been effectively re-designed around
such. This is the attitude taken by a number of games, as you note.

Garfield, however, went in a very different direction with Jyhad,
allowing you 90 copies of Lost in Crowds in a deck if you wanted - but
hamstringing you with repeat action modifiers, unnecessary stealth rules
and such like - the self-righting mechanism of a single concept deck,
designed to prevent abuse from having billions and billions of cards
whilst also giving Mr. Suitcase plenty of options.

Magic <-------------------------------------------------------> Jyhad
^
Limit | Encourage
The People Intelligent
Use Of Buy Lots Use of
Cards Of Cards Cards
(PROBLEM)

Jyhad was designed *entirely* in different directions to Magic. Trying
to go in reverse is kind of like saying "Well, I don't like Spanish as a
language. It needs to be more Russian." If you want to speak Russian,
move to Russia.

Is it more interesting to be bled out by an archetypal Malkavian sneak
bleed deck which uses Mind Rape, Govern the Unaligned, Spying Mission,
Night Moves, Lost in Crowds, Threats, Bonding, Scouting Mission,
Conditioning, Foreshadowing Destruction, Faceless Night and Command of
the Beast?

By sheer, unadulterated coincidence WITH NO DESIGN PLAN BEHIND IT *AT
ALL* (OH NO DEFINITELY NOT) this is also more likely to be most
effective way of building a deck under NL - and if people are playing
for fun, and playing to win, and playing intelligently......

I will, happily, build a Malkavian Stealth and Bleed deck under 4CL or
6CL and sit down and play it every single time, if you want. Would
seeing more and different pretty pictures saying "I BLEED YOU AND YOU
DIE BECAUSE WE'VE JUST FUCKED OVER YOUR ABILITY TO DEFEND YOURSELF
BECAUSE THE BLEED ARCHETYPE IS NOW AN ORDER OF MAGNITUDE MORE
POWERFUL"[0] make things any better?

If you're finding the game boring, NL really isn't the issue - people
are. Most specifically, your inability to build and decks that prise
people's flaws wide open and exploit them to the hilt, thus shifting the
meta-game for the other players to "Wow, this deck doesn't work so good
anymore.... I'd best fix it and play it better rather than the same-old
same-old they keep letting me do." Jyhad is a game requiring thought,
skill, charisma, discipline, intelligence, a little luck and sound
strategic brain. Using the ill-thought out, counter-productive xCL
crutch cuts away at all of this, all of what was designed, all of what
has evolved with new sets, all of what was intended. Why try and make
Jyhad into something that it's not?

Consider the game of chess versus the game of draughts. In draughts, we
only use half the squares, of one colour. In chess, we use all of them.
Should we try and turn one into the other to promote "variation",
ignoring strategy, design, intent and evolution?

Jyhad is Jyhad, as any other card game is any other card game[1]. I
accept and explore Jyhad for what it is, as an exciting, dynamic
strategic game with more facets to its play than you can shake a small
deciduous forest at. I accept Magic for what it is, too - which isn't
Jyhad.

[0] I paraphrase the reaction of many players regarding "I'm being bled
*again*", of course.

[1] Except Pokémon, of course, which is just an excuse to make money.
Semi-colon dash bracket etc.

>
> For tournament play (which I rarely have fun at anyway), I wholeheartedly
> agree that the rules are the rules and should be abided by. However, I take
> offense at the notion that customizing a game to suit one's social tastes is
> somehow inferior.

Social tastes are important, make no mistake, but they can change over
time. Let me tell you about our group here in Vienna. When we started
in '94 we played no limit, because we had only a handful cards, no
idea what this game was about, and the rulebook said nothing about any
form of CL. The decks at that time were "toolboxy" (we used to say
all-round decks), and things were *quite* balanced. It all started
when I put 12 Earth Meld in my Gangrel deck. The other players were
frustrated, they couldn't make much use of their combat cards, IG was
still yet to be *really* discovered (remember it was rare back then).
Comments were that it didn't seem right to allow so many untap cards
in a deck, and after a long debate we decided to *adopt the Magic rule
of 4CL*, as that was the only other noteable CCG at that time that all
of us knew. We then played for about 4 years that way, our group grew
to about 50 players, and *nobody* of the new ones asked why there was
a 4CL, most coming from Magic, it seemes natural to them. Of course
there were some cards and strategies that bewildered them: Corruption
being the most noteable card. :)
However, when the VEKN was formed, the NRA emerged, and a lot of
problem-cards were errataed (I only mention the 7/7 crisis... :)) we
slowly approached NCL very carefully, preparing our players and
eventually they have accepted that we only play NCL anymore.
You know, when all players in a group start from the same ground, a
lot of problems can be avoided. Players have now not 4 Wakes and 4
Forced Awakenings in their decks, but e.g. 7 Wakes and 1 Forced,
whichever suits their deck purpose more.
IMO, players only play with a CL, when they don't *see* the whole
picture. A player who understands that under NCL, he has the same *and
more* options in deckbuilding will be more willing to play NCL, and
when he realizes that under NCL he can defend himself quite easily
against the problem-cards (foremost S:CE, Untap-cards, and massive
stealth/bleed combos) he gets to like NCL. In our group NCL had the
effect, that players got a lot more creative in deckbuilding, and I've
never seen a hardcore stealth/bleed deck win a tournament final
(except when it's lucky and the predator of some ill-designed deck
that got by pure luck into the final round...).
One of the big differences between NCL and CL is that under CL there
was almost no choice in deck-building: any deck with Auspex packed
exactly 4 Telepathic Counter, 4 Telepathic Misdirection and 4 My
Enemy's Enemy along with 4 Wakes and 4 Forced Awakenings. Funny? No.
Boring? Yes.
Please also note that most decks that pack 30 copies of a single card
(e.g. a Brainwash Deck or a Night Moves deck) get *at best* 1 VP or
fail outright miserably.
As someone else said, the problem is not that some players put dozens
of copies of a single card into their deck, it's that the *other*
players in that group fail to exploit that weakness and come up with
ways to beat him.
Of course, it's the most easy way to go to just say "from now on we
use xCL, in order to hose that player and we don't have to adapt at
all.". But that's a false feeling of security. Even under a 4CL I can
pack *a lot* of stealth bleed: 4 Mask of 1K faces, 4 Lost in Crowds, 4
Faceless Night, 4 Cloak the Gathering, 4 Spying Mission. If I'm
feeling a little bit funky, I can even add 4 Psychic Veil! Now those
are 20 to 24 stealth cards. How is *that* different to say, 16 Cloak
the Gathering? It's even *better*, cause I can't play the same action
modifier twice in a single action. The same can be said about the
bleeding modifiers. 4 Conditioning, 4 Bonding, 4 Threats, spiced up
with 4 Govern the unaligned to begin with. Fun? No. Boring? Yes.
The defences against such a deck are rather limited under 4CL.

Ok, I guess this post is long enough right now. :) Thanks to all those
that read till the end. :)

Carl

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
Johan Lundstrom wrote:
>
> Frederick Scott <fre...@netcom.com> wrote:
>
> >As for NRA, it plugs a hole which exists in the constructed game from decks focused
> >on cards that allow untaps. It probably should be a real game rule but I suspect White
> >Wolf is dragging its feet because it's utterly unnecessary in the limited game. Saying
> >the game "as designed had some serious problems" is disingenuous.
>
> Since some people has used "the game was originally designed this way"
> as an argument against CLs, I thought it was worth pointing out that:
>
> a) There are lots of areas where we play the game differently than
> originally designed, and
> b) The original design had some serious flaws, meaning we shouldn't
> hold it as sacred.
>
> Saying "the game was originally designed not to have CLs" is not in
> itself an argumnet against them.

Well, yes, actually it is. Though you correctly point out that the original game
had flaws and consequently has been changed to ameliorate such flaws, that doesn't show
the lack of card limits is a flaw nor demonstrate any compelling need to change
it that way. Lots of rules were part of the original flawed game and do not require
changing.

The importance of the game not being designed to have card limits is intended to point
out that all the cards and all the other rules were designed as if the game has no card
limits. Adding card limits after the fact is awkward as it requires a careful
examination (which really should include a complete retesting) of every single existing
card in the game. In short, it's a extreme MAJOR alteration of the game in relation to
the environment in which the cards were playtested. NRA, by comparison, is a tweak.

I'm not suggesting that this automatically means a change on the order of card limits
could never improve a game designed without them. But it sure seems to be a good argument
against making changes on that order without being very sure what you're doing and exactly
why you're doing it. To me, limiting the influence of a relatively handful of cards can
not possibly justify applying blind limitations every single one of them. This is the whole
fallacy of the pro-CL argument in a nutshell, IMHO. "What's wrong with the game?", we ask.
The pro-CL argument can never possibly account for all the effects that slapping a limit on
every card has. For instance, is it good or bad to limit "Blood Puppy" to 4? Haven Uncovered?
Temple Hunting Ground? Sport Bike? Nephandus Mage? Gangrel Revel? And so on and so forth.
A case-by-case argument can not be made. So pro-CLers wave their hand over the whole process
and argue in vague generalities. The only way I can support this is if the result works
well, discernibly better than what we already have. All indications is that it doesn't,
except insofar as no players are ever required to get more than the CL worth of
the most expensive, rare cards to build any particular deck. No (pre-Sabbat-War) Legacy of
Pander decks. That sounds sort of egalitarian but others have pointed out the down side
for poor players: the same thing that shields them from too many opposing rare cards also
prevents them from using repeated, stock common cards that might (probably are, I think)
the more important thing in gaining an edge. So it isn't even necessarily egalitarian, either.

> However, I don't think CL's make the game a lot better. Although a
> card or mechanism that encouraged more diversity in decks would be
> nice.

It would be. However, this is not a mechanic that has anything directly to do with diversity
in deck types if that's what you mean by "diversity". So it seems strange to mention it.

Fred

> shove, the game system deals with it. You start playing with bleed
> bounce or Archon Investigation cards or some such if he doesn't cut it
> out.

So you encourage creativity through selective construction of a deck
that discourages a particular player's habitual use of a particular
strategy. "the game itself" never stands to encourage variety. As
you pointed out, it is up to other players to apply pressure to the
offending participant (within the context of the game, of course) and
get them to shift their habits. BTW, I put the word banner in quotes
to infer that it is an implied condition of participation within the
group, _not_ that it is some credo recited before each gaming
session...

> Since he should be playing to win, he should get tired of losing
> horribly every game until he learns to vary his deck (and therefore his
> path to victory) every game. It should not require the group to hoist
> any "banners".
>

You mistake my meaning. I get the impression that you think I want
players in a group to discourage banality merely by whining about it
to the offending player. Nothing could be further from the truth...

> > Ultimately, any encouragement of this source is rooted in a group's
> > social "pressure".
>
> Gosh I sure do vehemently disagree with this. Any encouragement of this
> source ought to come from the soundness of the game design and the strategy
> adopted by one's opponents..

As I point oput above, by selecting a tactic to foil a person's
habitual tactics, you are encouraging variety. The fact that it
occurs within the game does not preculde it from being a choice on
your part, and a social one at that. It is helped by the fact that
foil tactics typically help you win games, but to ignore the societal
aspect of this choice on your part isn't really helpful. Note that
the change in banal player comes out of _your_ choices. The game
gives you the context and tools to make such a choice (that's what
makes Jyhad such a great game), but it is not in itself somehow
directly involved in your decision to stymie that player.

By comparison, you could try the equally valid, but less socially
pressuring route of a tactic that runs parallel to the offending
player's (or possibly outpaces him at what he is doing). You'd likely
win your fair share, and take VP's from the offender, but would do so
without applying pressure to the banal player to change his tactics.

Alternatively, the simple habit of letting players know what caliber
of game you wish to play before starting it is another way that social
pressure is applied to play groups. Choosing to play a "tournament
caliber" game, or an "experimental" game as a group forces players to
get in line with their deck construction choices. Getting back to
what I was talking about with the CL/NCL debate, neither of these
choices directly affect these choices and pressures. they are created
within the group, by the group, and stand apart from the rules of the
game. that's why I said that CL/NCL and "variety" are two seperate
discussions.

Hope this clarifies my previous post...

DaveZ/Atom Weaver

Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson
Messages.Body:
On Wed, 04 Jul 2001 13:18:23 +1000, Kevin Lowe wrote:

>> >But it's no longer a competitive game of skill.

>The biggest "challenge" in 4CL deck design is finding enough cards that
>do the same thing to make a focused deck remotely possible. Then you
>toss in one of every master that rocks in the 4CL environment (turn for
>+1 stealth, sustained blood gain, turn to end combat etc). Whoopee.
>
>The challenge in no-L is to fine-tune the proportions of every card in
>the deck, to balance the proportions exactly how you want them and to
>ensure that your hand will flow smoothly.

Deck building is a poor test of skill because it's a simple matter to
copy a deck off the net. It's even easier than copying a book opening
in chess because you don't have to memorise it.

What I take most pleasure in is the skill of playing the game. A
focussed deck (i.e. many copies of few cards) is less interesting than
a more varied deck (toolbox or nCL) because fewer decisions are
required - the deck tends to play itself.

I hear it said that the most skilful format in Magic is the draft,
because it tests both deck-building and deck-play. This is the format
I like best for Vampire and I quite enjoyed the Sabbat War one I
played at Origins. I hauled back two cases of starters for Shadowfist
and Vampire and hope to use these to run more draft events here in the
UK.

I have a good format for such Shadowfist events already. Here's my
idea for a Vampire format using VTES/Jyhad starters. They have a
random mix of cards so some kind of draft is needed. The same idea
can be used for other games with similar randomized starters.

SUCCUBUS SEALED
---------------

1. Each player is given one starter which they may open.

2. The players sit at tables of 4-6.

3. An additional starter is opened on each table and laid out for
inspection.

4. Starting with the most charming player (the umpire gets a casting
vote), each player may take cards in rotation from the draft pool on
the table. Each card that is taken must be replaced by a card from
their stock, matching type for type - Vampire for Vampire, Master for
Master, Minion for Minion.

5. Draft trading continues until there is a round of passes. Players
may now draft from the pool without having to trade cards back. This
will exhaust the pool unless there are cards which no-one wants at any
price. These go to make a booby prize for the worst player.

6. Players may now tune their decks and commence play. It's probably
best if the players are reseated for the first round to discourage
counter-drafting and to encourage cooperative draft trading.

Andrew

a good deck and play it well. Thats why I consider folks from my area like
Noal, Aaron, and Bernie (just to name a few) to be skillful Jyhad players
because they dont just copy decks from the net. Each had a mostly-original
deck concept that was well put together and played well. (two of the three
qualified for Gen-Con)

Just my opinion of course,

Matt

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
"Andrew S. Davidson" wrote:
>
> On Wed, 04 Jul 2001 13:18:23 +1000, Kevin Lowe wrote:
> >The challenge in no-L is to fine-tune the proportions of every card in
> >the deck, to balance the proportions exactly how you want them and to
> >ensure that your hand will flow smoothly.
>
> Deck building is a poor test of skill because it's a simple matter to
> copy a deck off the net. It's even easier than copying a book opening
> in chess because you don't have to memorise it.

I strongly disagree. You can copy a decks from any number of sources but
so what? There's very few reliable sources in existence. Just because some
schmo declares he's won gads of tournaments with a deck doesn't mean it's
a good deck. He may be exaggerating about the wins or about the quality of
the competition. Even if he isn't, you don't know what the metagame he in
which he was playing looked like nor exactly how he used the cards he used
that led him to build in those particular cards. The latter is sometimes
obvious but sometimes it isn't.

Ultimately, deck lists are just suggestions, just like someone suggesting what
a card is good for or when and how to play it. Perhaps the information offered
can be a little more specific than a suggestion about when to draft a card or
when to play it, but the extremely specific information (exact numbers of various
cards in a deck) is precisely stuff that's highly controversial and may to
translate well in your environment or to your playing style.

> What I take most pleasure in is the skill of playing the game.

Not me. CCGs are about deck building. Often the actual play isn't that
interesting, particularly when someone's deck produces extremely strange
card ordering results (13 Bum's Rushes, 6 Haven Uncovereds, 16 of the 19
rush cards turn up in the second half of the deck) or when the metagame
and table order works strong in favor of one or two of the players.

Also, though games can easily be won or lost on the choice of when to play cards,
the actual wisdom of the choices usually tends to hinge on predicting what
you'll draw soon. Since I'm incapable of predicting what I'm about to topdeck,
I don't put a lot of stock in calling how individual games play out "skill".
(Though I can get cranky about it at times if I feel victimized too many games
in a row.)

> I hear it said that the most skilful format in Magic is the draft,
> because it tests both deck-building and deck-play.

I think deckbuilding with an unlimited pool of cards and drafting/deckbuilding from
a limited pool are two completely different skills. There are not so many decisions
to be made in the latter case; however, you have to make such decisions with no
practice whatsoever given the particular pool of cards you're offered and choose to
draft, which some of us find more challenging. I can't see any basis for stating
that one is a lot more skill than the other. One is a lot more easy to practice at
than the other since drafts are hard to arrange whereas regular constructed decks
can be built any time you're sitting next to your collection and tested in a wide
variety of situations. People who enjoy drafts and have the chance to engage in them
a lot will likely be much more practiced at them then others and I suspect that edge
will really show in a large tournament.

Fred

someone else's deck, and NOT someone in your playgroup. Let them look at

Yup. Shadowfist does have some elements of degenerate
deck-building-- virtually every new player goes through a love affair
with mono-Ascended cheese, but by and large, multiplayer dynamics
prevent any one deck archetype from dominating.
Doomtown's cheatin' and lowball draw mechanics make it so that
you either: (a) can't rely on a card coming out or (b) increase your
chances of being caught cheatin by playing too many of the same card.

: deck construction almost every time and since your easily cycle

: cards and your deck recycles when you run out, issues of luck
: are often minimized compared to other card games.

However, the original poster does make a point-- those that
play a lot of sealed have an advantage in this format. I think this
is perfectly okay-- along the lines of "those that play a lot of
constructed will have an advantage in that format." Worse yet (or
not), those that buy lots of cards have an advantage in that format,
too.
Speaking for myself, playing sealed draft Shadowfist is the
most fun i've had playing 'Fist in the last few months. Using, and
even coveting, subpar cards really defines the environment. I'd be
curious how Boot Hill starters would play in that format, given the
fixed presence of that low-value strike that increases the Fear Level
and has 2 CP.
I mentioned this briefly to Zev (getting back to Shadowfist for
a moment); he sort of shrugged and said Z-Man is going to focus on
expansions rather than randomized starters or a new basic set. I think,
given the discussion on the Doomtown list about the demise of DT, this
may be the wiser move from a financial standpoint. There are still
_some_ starters out there.

--
Eric

>Deck building is a poor test of skill because it's a simple matter to
>copy a deck off the net.

Not true.

Deck building comprises building a deck, certainly. However, a deck is
not just a deck. A deck is an extension of your play-style. If you
just copy a deck off the net, you have "failed" to get that tick on your
box unless you know that your play-style is so similar to that of the
player you are copying that it is effectively a deck you can play
exactly in the fashion intended.

Jyhad is a highly strategic game, but it is also a highly personal game
in a way I have never found The Other Game to be - partly, but not
solely, because of the strong social element. You have to know your own
limits in amongst other people, rather than in a 1-on-1 where social
elements are, effectively, irrelevant.
